extracted.intended_audience: general readers and students of political economy; legislators and policy-minded readers
extracted.subtask_short: economics dialogue on money and wealth
extracted.subtask_description: A pedagogical dialogue explaining fundamental political-economy principles about the nature of wealth, the function of money, and the harms of protectionism and fictitious money. Uses examples and thought experiments to show why cash is a medium/sign, not identical with real wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wealth defined as useful things produced by labour
rubrics_metrics.description: Wealth consists in the abundance and proper distribution of useful things (food, clothing, houses, fuel, books, conveyances, etc.) produced by nature and labour, not in the quantity of cash.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Emphasises that true riches are 'the mass of useful things which we produce by labour' and the 'result of all the efforts' to satisfy wants and tastes; policies should aim to increase useful goods, not merely monetary aggregates.

rubrics_metrics.name: Cash is a medium of exchange, not wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Cash serves only to facilitate exchanges; it is an intermediate agent that allows buying and selling independently of immediate barter, but it is not itself the thing that satisfies wants.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analogy: crowns are like counters under a candlestick—useful for transactions but not equivalent to the goods themselves. Policy and reasoning should distinguish instruments of exchange from real satisfactions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Increasing money supply alone does not increase real wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiplying crowns, paper money, or bank-notes without a corresponding increase in useful things will not increase real satisfactions; it only raises prices (depreciation) and leaves the mass of useful things unchanged.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains with the 'players' counter example: doubling counters without increasing the candlestick sum simply halves their purchasing power. Warns against believing that printing money will make everyone better off.

rubrics_metrics.name: Treating cash as a measure of value is a fallacy
rubrics_metrics.description: It is mistaken to regard cash as an unchanging measure of value (like yards or pounds) because the value of gold/silver (money) fluctuates like other commodities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When money's value changes, language misattributes change to other goods; this confusion causes policy errors. Policy analysis must account for money's own price fluctuations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Paper money and legal debasement cause depreciation and social harm
rubrics_metrics.description: Putting false money (paper, reduced-weight coins, assignats) into circulation inevitably produces depreciation (rising prices) that harms the poor and benefits those who can anticipate or speculate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Depreciation manifests unevenly and slowly; sharp traders adapt, while little tradesmen and workers are impoverished. Historical note: assignats and legal false money lead to civil unrest and long-term injury to the lower classes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Protectionism (prohibitive system) logically implies war and social costs
rubrics_metrics.description: If a legislator defines wealth as cash and seeks to prevent money leaving the country (forbidding exports, blocking imports), the logical policy consequences (custom-house officers, armies, taxes, colonies) lead to perpetual conflict and high social cost.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Shows chain of reasoning: forbidding imports => customs enforcement => other nations retaliate => military build-up and war. Highlights that such measures are extreme and self-defeating.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encouraging exports by prizes/tax incentives merely transfers wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: Policies that subsidize exports or impose taxes on domestic consumption to force sales abroad tend to lower domestic sellers' prices and effectively gift export gains to foreigners without creating new useful goods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: exporters constrained by competition lower prices proportionally, effectively transferring the benefit of prizes/taxes to foreign buyers. Encouraging exports this way does not necessarily increase national wealth.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exchange (division of labour) increases total production — trade is not zero-sum
rubrics_metrics.description: Differentiation of occupations and exchange increase the aggregate production of corn, wine, and meat; two nations (or individuals) can both prosper simultaneously by specialising and trading.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrated by Shem, Ham, Japhet example: specialization and liberty in exchange cause a rise in total useful things, contradicting Baconian/Montaignean axiom that one nation's gain is another's loss.

rubrics_metrics.name: A crown is a title to social services, not an addition to social wealth
rubrics_metrics.description: A coin (crown) testifies that the bearer has rendered a service to society and holds a claim to future services; transferring crowns redistributes claims but does not change society's real stock of satisfactions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Explains accounting-like nature: giving a crown for a service settles one person's claim and moves the title to another; societal wealth (real services) remains unchanged by mere transfers of money.

rubrics_metrics.name: An individual having more money does not imply the whole is richer without more goods or external inputs
rubrics_metrics.description: Individual increases in cash holdings (more crowns per person) do not make the whole nation richer unless backed by increased useful things—mines or beneficial trade—otherwise crowns simply change hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Uses the players' counter thought experiment and notes that only mines or import-driven acquisition of goods can raise the total of useful things; otherwise more money is only nominal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gold obtained by mining or favorable trade can increase real wealth only if it leads to useful imports or domestic production
rubrics_metrics.description: Gold from mines or gained by trade enriches a country insofar as it is exchanged for useful things (e.g., a locomotive) or substitutes for domestically-produced goods without causing worse distortions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Caveat: if gold merely increases money without productive use, it may depreciate and fail to increase enjoyments; a country could 'starve on heaps of gold' if money substitutes for productive effort.

rubrics_metrics.name: Policy experiments with money carry real risks and social costs
rubrics_metrics.description: Trying schemes like issuing paper money because 'there can be no risk' ignores that the failure of hope is a real misfortune and governments should not base tax or policy promises on uncertain monetary experiments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Warns against using expected success of monetary schemes to justify tax cuts or expenditures; emphasizes political and social fallout when such experiments produce depreciation and unequal effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inflation/depreciation effects are uneven and regressive
rubrics_metrics.description: The rise in prices following monetary depreciation is neither instantaneous nor uniform; businesspeople and speculators adjust quickly, while wages and prices faced by laborers lag, making the poor bear the burden.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Policy-makers should recognise distributional effects of monetary changes: inflation widens the gap between rich and poor and can take generations for the lower classes to recover lost ground.

rubrics_metrics.name: Legal debasement and enforced acceptance of reduced-value money are equivalent to counterfeit
rubrics_metrics.description: Forcing people to accept lighter coins or paper that represents a higher nominal value is morally and economically analogous to putting false money into circulation and leads to the same depreciation problems.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example given: making a piece weigh half as much but still calling it a 'franc' produces the same mischief as issuing assignats; all arguments for assignats parallel those for legal debasement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Confusing money with wealth spawns related fallacies (hatred of capital, gratuitous credit)
rubrics_metrics.description: The root confusion between money and real wealth gives rise to other erroneous doctrines—prohibitionist, colonial, hostility toward capital, and belief in gratuitous credit or easy remedies like paper money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Signals further topics to examine (hatred of capital, gratuitous credit) as consequences of the same foundational error; policy analysis should address these linked fallacies together.
